en: They have begun to share together
The pleasures of this deceitful world until death,
To die when fate overtakes them,
And, digging a deep grave and stamping it firm,
For one to bury the other.
They have united and begun their revels,
And all the wealth they gathered
They have heaped together in one place.
They have made great Talas a fortress
And hero Kenen its lord.
If we do not go and crush
The crowns of those men,
If we do not drive out the ancient fury
Of Ebegey and Kögöy,
Of hero Akjoltoy and Kenen—
Those four guardians of the people—
If we do not strike first,
And find a way to settle the score,
If we do not block their traveled roads
And drive out every last one of their people,
Breaking their steadfast backs
And stilling their unruly hearts,
Driving spears into their farthest reaches,
Destroying all who resist,
And making their mighty men burn;
If we do not enslave that wretched nation
And divide them by measure of the lash—
The messenger has come saying Kenen is renowned,
Bringing word
That an enemy ready to fight you
Now stands prepared.
If we do not advance and block his road,
Scatter all he has acquired,
And overrun his settlements,
Then slaughter the thoroughbreds bred in Beijing—
This is the secret your lord now declares.
Braid the thoroughbreds’ manes.
If you take off your boots, stretch out your legs,
And lie at ease in careless peace,
Then within five or six years
The renowned gray wolf Kenen—
The infidel who devastated the people,
Whose wrathful power spells the end of the age—
Look upon him here in Beijing!
Will he remain without picking a quarrel,
Will he stop without trading insults?
If he rules the people and commands a nation,
Will he not seek revenge upon
The Chinese nation of forty khans
For his khan-father, blood-shedding Manas?!
The great lords of the Chinese realm,
Finding Chyngteñir’s judgment fitting,
The strong men clad in armor,
The heroes wearing mail,
The champions dressed in stone-hard armor,
The boundless men in quilted coats,
The warriors who know their own worth,
Despairing of their lives like flies,
The many seething dignitaries,
Saying that an edict had come from the khan,
Ran up and down,
Surged right and left in turmoil,
Young and old together—
All of Kakan and Beijing—
The whole people now heaved like a flood.
He made ready in wrath;
Chyngteñir was a mighty lord.
Taking the aspect of a blue-maned lion,
His voice thundered like the sky,
He loomed like a gray mountain range;
Any man who tried to judge him
Would lose the thread of his reason.
His fierce mustache appeared
Like the scree of Mount Kap;
His eyes were like blazing flame,
His jewel button was as large as a fist—
Such was his splendid appearance.
The countless Chinese facing him
Could not bear to look him in the face;
Whoever saw him despaired of life,
And knew him for a blue-maned lion.
Such was Chyngteñir, khan of the Chinese realm;
Such was the command he gave.
From before that formidable hero-lord
The envoys came forth,
The imposing appraisers:
Critics who could judge from afar,
Spies who ranged across foreign lands,
Men who worked through cunning,
Men who knew how to gauge a people,
Men who loaded merchandise on camels,
Who traded gold and silver,
Traveling as merchants,
Who among the Kyrgyz of Ala-Too
Drew out their hidden secrets,
Who kindled fire between peoples,
Who watched from outside to learn
The extent and strength of a nation.
The keenest judge among these observers,
The critic Zhelzhetpes, arrived.
He gauged the strength of the Kyrgyz
And observed their gathered people.
To the khan and lord Chyngteñir
He reported everything without omission:
“I observed Kenen carefully,
That lion and tiger of a warrior;
I studied the hero closely.
He is dark without and resolute within.
He will not fold his hands and submit,
Saying, ‘We are your slaves.’
He is no boy who will yield to fortune,
Nor some witless nobody.
They are not a people who will submit to being driven,
Like the Shibe and Torgout;
Nor are they a multitude like the Chinese.
The Kyrgyz nation is no grass to be mown.
Hero-lord, heed my words.
Let us send between us as envoy
An unerring, broad-jawed orator,
A man whose speech is sweet as sugar,
Whose skill surpasses the wisdom of an age.
Let us send an envoy between us,
And test their strength through words.
With reason and speech,
With strategy and skill,
Let us learn the measure of their strength.
Without quarreling or raising strife,
Let us mount the throne in triumph.
Let us cast a chilling lasso
Over the swift horse they would never surrender,
And take their graceful daughters
As plunder by such means.”
Thus spoke Zhelzhetpes,
Whose wisdom none could fathom,
The finest cultivator of reason,
A clear-sighted sage,
One who, among Chinese and Kyrgyz alike,
Would come first in any contest.
The wise man sharpened his words further;
Zhelzhetpes spoke on in this way.
Wrapped in a mottled blue robe,
The fearsome Chyngtengir, behold,
Raged like a blue-gray tiger,
And girded on his blue steel blade;
His eyes blazed like a boar's:
— Damn you, Zhelzhetpes!
Who should listen to such words of yours?
Let the dark night listen,
Let beast and living soul listen;
These words that you have spoken—
Let four-footed cattle hear them,
Let the dug black grave hear them,
Let the broad black earth hear them!
When I sent you to survey the land,
You were one of my capable men,
Yet you have always gone about
Feeling pity for the Kyrgyz.
You have become a hindrance to my work,
A wrecker among my men;
It seems you mean to carry this through,
To the stammering Kyrgyz themselves
It seems you intend to go!
You are no envoy, but a land surveyor,
A goldsmith who deceives this nation!
You yourself would ruin the people,
You are the very eye of treachery.
Every word you say points elsewhere;
If I leave you alive,
You will spoil every little undertaking.
Without once looking back toward China,
You hasten toward the Kyrgyz!
If you keep this up, Zhelzhetpes,
You will set fire to my heart
And bring strife upon Beijing.
From time to time, in every age,
An enemy like you has risen within,
Destroyed my people,
And plunged into darkest night
The lofty honor I possessed.
So saying, Chyngtengir
Thundered like a lightning bolt.
When he saw Chyngtengir's wrath,
His brow twitched and his teeth ground;
How could he answer back?
His cunning tongue fell silent.
Though there was no rope or cord,
His hands and feet seemed helplessly bound.
Then, speaking softly but firmly,
Zhelzhetpes began his reply:
You are a warrior, mighty Chyngtengir;
You may cut off this wretched head.
But a people, its treasure, its homes—
You will gain nothing by acting so.
A khan's ambition is a maddened camel;
If it tramples you, it will finish you.
Yesterday, black-jowled Zulpukor—
You drew Zulpukor and brandished it;
Making men lick the sword's edge,
You scattered a thousand of us
And sent us against the white-capped people.
We watched them from without and judged them,
We ranged their land and examined it closely.
They too are sons of men.
Kenen is indeed a mighty hero,
And the army he has mustered stands ready.
Ala-Too is no land cheaply won;
Without spilling blood and waging strife,
Without splitting lungs in single combat,
He is not one to surrender his people.
His courage is no less than yours.
One young lad stands in his support,
The forty chiltens and holy Khizr are his true aid,
Ever present before his face.
He is one of the proven warriors,
A man endowed with sacred grace.
Two twin lions, two champions,
Alym and Kulansaryk,
Are lion-hearted sons he has.
However I look at him from every side,
Kenen is no son to be cheaply taken.
He is no foe you can seize as spoil
And make into your plaything;
His is no people of forty scattered tribes
That you may slaughter and butcher,
Nor am I there in his hands.
If you face them and level spears,
Blood will surely be spilled;
If you meet them man to man,
They will test the limits of your strength.
Use force, and they will fight.
The Kyrgyz warrior's father was a lion;
They strike fiercely and raise battle.
Those pass-ridden mountains are a hell;
A foe that splits lungs and severs heads—
Measured rightly, that is the Kyrgyz!
I have told you truly what I saw:
If you provoke war, you will slaughter them like sheep,
But if you stiffen in wrath,
You will only bring ruin on yourself.
That would be sheer folly;
Know this and take heed.
Thus Zhelzhetpes spoke,
Offering words as a warning,
Driving them home and speaking firmly:
My champion, listen to me.
When they heard this counsel,
The chiefs of the Kaldai said,
Are his words not reasonable?
If he rejects the mediator,
The khan's good fortune will depart;
The khan's strength will be broken.
If he torments the innocent,
The people's spirit will be corrupted.
What fault is there in this advice?
So Suradai asked him:
— Heed what the envoy says;
